explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but the verse goes the other way. After the LORD roars from Zion and raises His voice from Jerusalem, Amos says the pastures of the shepherds mourn. Amos is a sheepherder himself, so I think those pastures hit close to home for him. A pasture throwing a party would be a nice picture, but that's not what he sees.

That's it. Amos says the pastures of the shepherds mourn, and the summit of Carmel withers. So when the LORD roars, the land feels it. Even the grass is not having a good day, and Amos is a sheepherder, so I think those pastures matter to him.

I get the hope, friend, but sparing isn't in this verse. The LORD says He will break down the gates of Damascus and cut off the ruler from the Valley of Aven. The one who wields the scepter in Beth-eden gets the same word. Nobody on this list is getting a surprise exemption.

Servants never come up here, baker. The LORD says He will cut off the ruler from the Valley of Aven and the one who wields the scepter in Beth-eden. That's the word He uses for them. It's a different outcome from becoming somebody's servant.

explanations.answer: Exiled them and handed them to Edom
explanations.explanation: That's the charge. The LORD says Gaza "…exiled a whole population, delivering them up to Edom." Notice it's a whole population, not a few people here and there. That's why Gaza is on the list.

explanations.answer: Stole all their flocks and herds
explanations.explanation: Amos is a sheepherder, so I see why flocks came to mind, friend. But the LORD never mentions flocks or herds in Gaza's charge. He says they exiled a whole population and delivered them up to Edom. The charge is about people.

explanations.answer: Burned their homes to the ground
explanations.explanation: Fire does show up in this passage, baker, but it's what the LORD sends on Gaza's walls, not Gaza's charge. Gaza's charge is that they exiled a whole population and delivered them up to Edom. That's the line to hold onto.

Other way around, friend. The LORD says, “…and the remnant of the Philistines will perish…” says the Lord GOD. A remnant is the leftover group, and this verse says it perishes too. It's easy to miss because the cities get named first, and then the remnant gets its own line.

That's the one. The LORD says Tyre "…delivered up a whole congregation of exiles to Edom…" It sounds a lot like the charge against Gaza, and that's what you noticed. Two cities handing people over to Edom, and both are on the list.

Nice guess, friend, but treasures aren't what the verse says. The LORD says Tyre delivered up a whole congregation of exiles to Edom. It's people again, and not a single treasure chest is in the charge.

No chariots in this verse, baker. The LORD says Tyre delivered up a whole congregation of exiles to Edom. The charge is about people being handed over, not gear. Horses would have been an easier charge to hear, I think.

You got it. The LORD says Tyre delivered up exiles to Edom "…and broke a covenant of brotherhood." So the charge has two parts, and the second is about a covenant Tyre broke. A covenant is a serious promise, and the LORD names this one as a covenant of brotherhood.

That's not in Tyre's charge, friend. The LORD says Tyre delivered up a whole congregation of exiles to Edom and broke a covenant of brotherhood. The second part is about a promise, and it doesn't mention mocking. I'd stick to the words the LORD actually says.

Gilead does show up in this passage, baker, but in Damascus's charge. Damascus threshed Gilead with sledges of iron. Tyre's second charge is that it broke a covenant of brotherhood. Same prophecy, different nation, so I get how they swapped.

Not quite, friend. The LORD says Edom's "…anger raged continually, and his fury flamed incessantly." That is not a flare-up that cooled off. It's anger that kept going, and the LORD says Edom stifled all compassion too.

Right, baker. The LORD says, “his anger raged continually, and his fury flamed incessantly.” Continually and incessantly are the key words, so it didn't flare once and fade. Edom stifled all compassion, and this anger never let up either.

A fallen king doesn't show up in the Ammonites' charge, friend. The LORD says they did it in order to enlarge their territory. It's a heavy charge, and the reason is stated plainly. I'd keep to what He says.

Moab gets its own charge a bit later, baker, and it's a different one. For the Ammonites, the LORD says they did it in order to enlarge their territory. This is one of the heavy parts of the passage. The reason is in the verse.

explanations.answer: He will go into exile with his princes
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD says their king will go into exile, he and his princes together. The ones at the top don't get a separate exit. They go together, and that's the whole picture.

explanations.answer: He will flee alone to the desert
explanations.explanation: Alone is the part that doesn't fit, friend. The LORD says the king will go into exile, he and his princes together. So he has company, and it's his own princes. The desert isn't in the verse either.

explanations.answer: He will surrender and keep his throne
explanations.explanation: Keeping a throne isn't in this verse, baker. The LORD says the Ammonite king will go into exile with his princes together. A throne is hard to keep from another country. The verse gives exile, not a surrender.

Yes, friend. The LORD says Moab "…burned to lime the bones of Edom’s king." It's a hard charge. It's also a reminder that Edom shows up in this passage as a nation with a charge, and also as someone who was wronged.

That's it, baker. The LORD says, “I will cut off the ruler of Moab and kill all the officials with him…” says the LORD. So it's not only the ruler, the officials are included. The first half of the statement was true, and the second half is what flips it.
